content.explanation: Only 10th graders are being considered, so use the 10th-grade row: $50$ of the $80$ 10th graders chose a packed lunch. The probability is $\frac{50}{80} = \frac{5}{8}$, or $0.625$.

content.stem: A bag contains $6$ red marbles, $9$ blue marbles, and $5$ green marbles. If one marble is chosen at random, what is the probability that it is not blue?
content.explanation: There are $6 + 9 + 5 = 20$ marbles. The marbles that are not blue are the $6$ red and $5$ green ones, $11$ in all. The probability is $\frac{11}{20}$.

distractorRationales.label: A

content.stem: A fair six-sided die, with faces numbered $1$ through $6$, is rolled twice. What is the probability that the sum of the two rolls is $10$ or greater?
content.explanation: There are $6 \times 6 = 36$ equally likely ordered outcomes. The ones with a sum of $10$ or more are $(4,6)$, $(5,5)$, $(6,4)$, $(5,6)$, $(6,5)$, and $(6,6)$: $6$ outcomes. The probability is $\frac{6}{36} = \frac{1}{6}$.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is $\frac{3}{36}$, which counts only sums greater than $10$ and leaves out the three ways to get exactly $10$.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is $\frac{4}{36}$, which counts $(4,6)$ and $(6,4)$ as one outcome and $(5,6)$ and $(6,5)$ as one outcome; order matters when listing the $36$ outcomes.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This treats the $11$ possible sums, $2$ through $12$, as equally likely, but they are not.

content.stem: A box contains $8$ batteries, $3$ of which are dead. Two batteries are selected at random without replacement. What is the probability that both selected batteries work?
content.explanation: $5$ of the $8$ batteries work. The probability that the first battery works is $\frac{5}{8}$. If it does, $4$ working batteries remain among $7$, so the probability that the second also works is $\frac{4}{7}$. Multiply: $\frac{5}{8} \times \frac{4}{7} = \frac{20}{56} = \frac{5}{14}$.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is $\frac{5}{8} \times \frac{5}{8}$, which assumes the first battery is put back before the second is drawn.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is the probability that exactly one of the two batteries works: $2 \times \frac{5}{8} \times \frac{3}{7} = \frac{15}{28}$.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is the probability that only the first battery works, ignoring the second draw.

content.stem: In a certain town, $40\%$ of households own a dog, $25\%$ own a cat, and $10\%$ own both a dog and a cat. If a household that owns at least one of these pets is selected at random, what is the probability that it owns a dog?
content.explanation: First find the share of households that own at least one of the pets. Adding $40\% + 25\%$ counts the $10\%$ that own both twice, so subtract it once: $40\% + 25\% - 10\% = 55\%$. All $40\%$ of dog owners are in this group. The probability is $\frac{40}{55} = \frac{8}{11}$.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is the probability that any household in the town owns a dog; the selection is only among households with at least one of the pets.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This uses $40\% + 25\% = 65\%$ for households with at least one pet, counting the households that own both pets twice.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is $\frac{30}{55}$, which counts only households that own a dog but no cat; households that own both also own a dog.

content.stem: The partially completed table shows the juniors and seniors in a school's student council and whether each owns a car. For a senior on the council selected at random, the probability of owning a car is $0.45$. If a member of the council is selected at random, what is the probability that the member owns a car?
content.explanation: Let $s$ be the number of seniors. The $18$ seniors who own a car are $45\%$ of the seniors, which gives the equation $0.45s = 18$. Divide both sides by $0.45$ to get $s = \frac{18}{0.45}$, which simplifies to $s = 40$. (As a check, $0.45 \cdot 40 = 18$.) The council has $30 + 40 = 70$ members, and $12 + 18 = 30$ of them own a car. The probability is $\frac{30}{70}$, which simplifies to $\frac{3}{7} \approx 0.4286$.

content.stem: The table shows the results of a quality inspection of $1{,}500$ items made at three factories. If an item that was not made at Factory A is selected at random, what is the probability that it is defective?
content.explanation: Only items from Factories B and C count: $400 + 500 = 900$ items. Of these, $18 + 15 = 33$ are defective. The probability is $\frac{33}{900} = \frac{11}{300}$.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is $\frac{33}{1500}$, which divides by all $1{,}500$ items instead of only the $900$ not made at Factory A.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This adds the defect rates of the two factories, $\frac{18}{400} + \frac{15}{500}$; probabilities for different groups can't be added this way.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is $\frac{33}{45}$, the probability that a defective item was not made at Factory A, which reverses the condition.
